title: Your practice so far

lines: ONE RULE: ONLY WHAT YOU DO.
cards: One question, quick to ask and harder than it sounds. Not what practice you admire. Not what you plan to start on Monday.
What did you actually do yesterday that you'd call practice? A breath before a meal. A line said under your breath.

A slow walk. A pause before a sharp reply. This path has handed you pieces for four years, and this year alone brought Tao Te Ching chapters, Montaigne's attempts, Thoreau's woods and a tour of the world's schools.
Some pieces stuck. Some went back in the box. Today is an inventory, with one rule: only what you actually do.

teach.h: ADMIRED IS NOT THE SAME AS DONE.
teach.b: First, admired is not the same as done. A shelf can hold books you meant to read, and a mind can hold practices you meant to keep. That's not a failing.
The admired list is a wish; the done list is a map, and you can only start a trip from where you really are. Second, an old check.
This year brought Zengzi, a student of Confucius, who in the Analects examines himself every day on three points. Had he been loyal in working for others? Trustworthy with friends?
And the third: had he practiced what he was taught? Not learned. Practiced.
The Analects puts the weight on doing.
Third, small counts. In the book of Zechariah, in a passage about a building just begun, the prophet asks: "For who hath despised the day of small things?"
A practice that has become habit can be so quiet you forget to list it: the breath before you answer, the cup of tea drunk slowly on purpose, the walk without your phone. Those belong on the list.

teach.h: A SHORT LIST IS AN HONEST LIST.
teach.b: Fourth, a short list is an honest list.
If what you actually do fits on one line, that line is worth more than a page of plans. It's real, it's yours, and it already works in your life. Tomorrow looks ahead.
Today, only the ground under your feet.

how: People who keep a personal spiritual practice often take stock at the end of a season by writing down what they actually do each day and week, rather than what they hope to do, and build from that list.

games.q: what does “your practice so far” mean?
o: a plan for the practices you'll start next year
the practices you actually do now, not the ones you admire
every practice you've read about across four years

games.q: your practice so far: tap the pairs.
p: did I practice what I was taught?
who hath despised the day of small things?

s: Zengzi's third daily check asks whether he had learned enough
it asks whether he had practiced what he was taught. not learned: practiced.
only long, formal practices belong on the list
small counts: a breath before you answer, tea drunk slowly on purpose, a walk without your phone.
Zechariah asks who has despised the day of small things
"For who hath despised the day of small things?" small counts.

games.q: making your list, you remember a long meditation you love the idea of, though you haven't done it in months. what do you do?
o: put it at the top; it's the one that matters most.
leave it off; today's list is only what you actually do.
throw the whole list away; it's too short.
games.why: today's one rule: only what you actually do. the admired list is a wish; the done list is a map, and a short list is an honest one.

practice: Walk back through yesterday slowly, from waking to sleep, like rewinding a film, and each time you meet something you'd call practice, a pause, a prayer, a walk, a kind word said on purpose, note it and keep going.
Leave off the things you only meant to do, and if the list is short, let it be short. If you pray, put prayer on the list exactly as it really happens.

wordCard.voice: Your practice so far. Not the practices you admire, but the ones you actually do, gathered from four years of pieces. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese xi, to practice or rehearse: the word in Zengzi's third check (Analects 1.4).

carryVoice: Your line: what I do. However short, it's the ground everything else will stand on. Same time tomorrow.

sources.ref: Analects 1.4 (Zengzi examines himself daily on three points: loyalty in working for others, trustworthiness with friends, practicing what he was taught)
